newsitem.title: INDIA: India budget seen going down with Gowda government.
newsitem.headline: India budget seen going down with Gowda government.

text.p: The chances of parliament approving India's pro-market 1997/98 (April-March) budget faded on Friday as the country's ruling coalition faced near certain defeat in a vote of confidence, politicians and analysts said.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition called the vote in parliament to end a political crisis after his minority government lost vital Congress party support.
"The budget was appreciated by all sections of the society," Deve Gowda said after moving the confidence motion on Friday.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram told reporters during a break in the parliamentary debate that he remained confident the budget would be passed.
But hopes of salvaging the budget, welcomed by business and political circles as a fillip for the economy, receded as Gowda's rivals readied to defeat the vote.
"There is no hope of the budget being passed. I would expect a vote-on-account for a few more months," constitutional lawyer K.K. Venugopal told Reuters.
The vote-on-account is a bill that temporarily provides money to fund government programmes until the budget is passed.
Parliament has to approve the proposals before the end of May.
"I think a budget can wait..." senior Congress leader Priya Ranjan Das Munshi said in response to Gowda's speech on Friday.
The budget, presented by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on February 28, proposes to slash corporate taxes, lower income tax and reduce import tariffs.
The plans revived stock markets and enthused business and industry. But their future was thrown into doubt when Congress withdrew its make-or-break support for Deve Gowda's coalition on March 30.
Most political parties have promised not to let the political crisis derail the budget, but members of the ruling alliance have linked its fate to their survival.
"If the government falls, how can be the budget be approved?" said a United Front politician, who did not want to be identified.
Soon after Deve Gowda moved the trust vote in parliament, the Bombay stock index tumbled 45.41 points, but later rebounded strongly and was up 1.27 percent, or 45.87 points, at 0840 GMT.

Industry leaders say that if the budget is not approved by parliament and the country heads for fresh elections, the economy will lose momentum and investment plans, including the flow of foreign funds, will be stalled.
"If there are elections, it would be a great setback to foreign investors," Tushar Sarda, president and chief executive officer of Daewoo Securities, told Reuters.
With both the Congress and the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party directing their deputies to vote against the government, the fate of the alliance seems to have been sealed.
The coalition controls 178 seats in the 542-member lower house, the Congress 140, and the BJP and its allies 193.
